description: Enjoying, understanding and responding to stories, poems and plays from India and around the world. Children move from listening and retelling to analysing character, genre, theme and the craft of authors.

lessons.title: Who, Where, What?
objectives: Name the characters and setting of a story
Say what happened at the beginning, middle and end
prerequisites: Can listen to a short story
explanation: Every story has characters — the people or animals in it. It has a setting — the place where it happens, like a forest or a kitchen.
Things happen in a story, one after another. Something happens at the beginning, something exciting in the middle, and the story finishes at the end.
When we remember who, where and what happened, we can tell the story again in our own words. That is called retelling.

vocabulary.meaning: a person or animal in a story
where a story happens
the start
the finish

examples: In "The Thirsty Crow", the character is a crow and the setting is a hot, dry place with a pot.
Beginning: the crow is thirsty. Middle: it drops pebbles in the pot. End: it drinks the water.

story.title: The Thirsty Crow
story.text: On a hot day, a crow was very thirsty. It found a pot with a little water at the bottom, but its beak could not reach. The crow had an idea! It dropped pebbles into the pot, one by one. The water rose higher and higher, until the crow could drink. Clever crow!

activities.prompt: Who is the main character in The Thirsty Crow?
Put the story in order
What did the crow put in the pot?
The crow gave up and flew away.

thinking: What else could the crow have done to get the water?
Why do you think the crow did not give up?
speaking: Retell The Thirsty Crow to a grown-up using a cup, water and pebbles.

project.title: Be the Clever Crow
steps: Pour a little water into the glass
Mark where the water is
Drop pebbles in one at a time
Watch the water rise
Tell the story while you do it
project.safety: Use a wide, stable plastic cup instead of a tall glass and large stones that cannot be swallowed; do not use marbles or small pebbles with young children. Supervise the activity and keep objects away from mouths.

assessment.prompt: Where did the crow find water?
Order
The water went up when the pebbles went in.

mastery: Names characters and setting of a familiar story
Retells a short story with beginning, middle and end
Answers simple "why" questions about a story

lessons.title: Clap, Stomp and Rhyme
objectives: Join in with a rhyme using actions
Hear the rhyming words in a poem
explanation: Poems often have rhymes — words that sound the same at the end, like star and far, or bee and tree.
Poems also have a beat, like a heart: da-DUM, da-DUM. We can clap or stomp to the beat.
Many rhymes repeat lines again and again. Repeating helps us remember the poem and join in.

vocabulary.meaning: words arranged with rhythm, often rhyming
words that end with the same sound
the steady rhythm we can clap to

examples: "Twinkle, twinkle, little star, how I wonder what you are" — star and are rhyme.
"Machli jal ki rani hai" is a Hindi rhyme many children in India know.

story.title: The Rhyming Parade
story.text: In Word Woods, the animals had a rhyming parade. "I'm a cat in a hat!" called the cat. "I'm a frog on a log!" croaked the frog. "I'm a bee in a tree!" buzzed the bee. Olu the owl clapped the beat, and everyone stomped along.

activities.prompt: Match the rhyming words
Which word rhymes with "sun"?
"Ball" and "tall" rhyme.
Which word does NOT rhyme with "cake"?

thinking: Why do you think little children love rhymes?
Can you make up a silly rhyme for your name?
speaking: Say a favourite rhyme to a grown-up with actions, and point out two words that rhyme.

project.title: Rhyme Time Shaker Show
steps: Make a shaker by putting rice in a bottle and taping it shut
Choose a rhyme you know
Shake on each beat as you say it
Perform it for your family
project.safety: Use a sturdy plastic bottle with a secure cap, tape it closed with an adult, and check that no small pieces can escape. Do not put rice or beans in the mouth.

assessment.prompt: Which rhymes with "dog"?

Rhyme pairs

lessons.title: The Hare and the Tortoise
objectives: Retell a fable and identify its moral
Explain how a character's actions led to the ending
explanation: A fable is a short story, often with animals, that teaches a lesson. The lesson is called the moral.
Many famous fables are credited to Aesop, a storyteller from ancient Greece. India has its own great collection of fables, the Panchatantra.
In fables, what characters do leads to what happens to them. A boastful character often learns a lesson; a patient or clever character often succeeds.

vocabulary.meaning: a short story that teaches a lesson
the lesson of a story
to show off about yourself

examples: The Hare and the Tortoise: moral — slow and steady wins the race.
The Lion and the Mouse: moral — even small friends can be a big help.

story.title: The Hare and the Tortoise
story.text: A speedy hare laughed at a slow tortoise. "Let's race!" said the tortoise. The hare raced ahead, then thought, "I have plenty of time," and lay down for a nap. The tortoise kept walking, step by step, never stopping. When the hare woke up, the tortoise was crossing the finish line!

activities.prompt: Why did the hare lose?
The moral is…
options: Slow and steady wins the race

activities.prompt: Put the fable in order
The tortoise stopped to rest.

thinking: Was the hare a bad animal, or did he just make a mistake?
When in your life is "slow and steady" a good idea?
speaking: Tell the fable from the tortoise's point of view to someone.

project.title: Fable Finger Puppets
steps: Draw a hare and a tortoise and cut them out
Tape them into rings for your fingers
Act out the race
Say the moral at the end
project.safety: Use child-safe scissors with adult supervision. Keep small paper pieces away from younger children who may put them in their mouths.

assessment.prompt: A fable usually teaches a…

The Panchatantra is a collection of fables from India.

lessons.title: What Will Happen Next?
objectives: Make predictions using clues from the story
Check and change predictions as the story continues
explanation: Good readers think ahead. They make a prediction: a smart guess about what will happen next, based on clues.
Clues come from the title, pictures, what characters say, and what usually happens in stories like this one.
As we keep reading, we check: was I right? If not, we change our prediction. Being wrong is fine — it means the author surprised us!

vocabulary.meaning: a smart guess about what will happen
a hint
a traditional story passed down by telling

examples: Title: "The Clever Minister" — clue that someone will be clever.
A character says "I will trick him!" — clue that a trick is coming.

story.title: Birbal and the Crow Count
story.text: Emperor Akbar asked, "Birbal, how many crows live in this city?" Everyone wondered how anyone could know. Birbal smiled and said, "Nine thousand and ninety-nine, Your Majesty. If there are more, some are visiting relatives. If fewer, some have gone to visit theirs!" Akbar laughed at the clever answer.

activities.prompt: Akbar asks a very hard question. What do you predict Birbal will do?
Which is a clue for a prediction?
options: the colour of the cover only

activities.prompt: Good readers change their prediction if new clues appear.
Birbal's answer was…

thinking: Could anyone really count all the crows in a city? Why was Birbal's answer clever?
Is it more fun when a story surprises you?
speaking: Stop a story halfway and predict the ending to a grown-up, giving one clue for your idea.

project.title: Prediction Story Box
steps: A grown-up puts three objects from a story in a box
Look at them and predict what the story is about
Listen to the story

assessment.prompt: A prediction is…

lessons.title: What Is This Character Like?
objectives: Describe a character's traits using evidence
Explain how a character changes during a story
explanation: A character trait is what a character is like inside: brave, greedy, kind, lazy, honest. Traits are shown through what characters say, do and think.
Feelings change during a story, and sometimes traits change too. A greedy character may learn to share by the end.
To describe a character, give evidence: "The king was greedy because he wanted everything he touched to turn to gold."

vocabulary.meaning: what a character is like inside
proof from the story
when a character becomes different

examples: King Midas is greedy (he asks for everything to turn to gold), then regretful (his food and daughter turn to gold).
The lion is proud, but becomes grateful when the mouse frees him.

story.title: The Golden Touch
story.text: In an old Greek story, King Midas wished that everything he touched would turn to gold. At first he was delighted — gold chairs, gold roses! But then his bread turned to gold, and he could not eat. When he hugged his daughter, she turned to gold too. Midas wept and begged for the wish to be taken away. He learned that love matters more than gold.

activities.prompt: At the start, King Midas was…
Which is evidence he changed?
options: He begged for the wish to be taken away.

activities.prompt: Match the action to the trait
Characters can change during a story.

thinking: Why do you think authors make characters change?
Would you want the golden touch? What would you wish for instead?
speaking: Describe a character from a favourite book using two traits and evidence for each.

project.title: Character Profile Card
steps: Draw the character in the middle
Write three traits around them
Add evidence from the story for each
Draw an arrow showing how they changed

assessment.prompt: A character trait is…
King Midas learned that…
We find evidence for traits in what characters say and do.

mastery: Identifies traits supported by evidence
Describes character change across a story

lessons.title: Cinderella Around the World
objectives: Compare two versions of a similar story
Explain how setting and culture shape a story
explanation: Some stories are told in many countries, each with its own twist. Stories about a kind, mistreated person who is rewarded — like Cinderella — appear in many cultures.
An early recorded version is the Chinese tale of Ye Xian, written down over a thousand years ago. Other versions come from Egypt, France, Germany and many other places.
When we compare versions, we look for what is the same (the plot pattern) and what is different (the setting, the magic helper, the ending).

context.text: The story of Ye Xian was recorded by the Chinese writer Duan Chengshi in the 9th century CE. Folklorists group stories like this under a shared "tale type" because similar plots appear in many cultures.

vocabulary.meaning: one way of telling a story
find what is the same and different
the way of life of a group of people

examples: In the French version, a fairy godmother helps; in Ye Xian, a magical fish helps.
The lost shoe is a glass slipper in one version and a golden shoe in another.

story.title: Ye Xian and the Magic Fish
story.text: Long ago in China, a kind girl named Ye Xian was treated unkindly by her stepmother. Her only friend was a beautiful fish. When the stepmother harmed the fish, its bones still granted Ye Xian's wishes. She went to a festival in a cloak of kingfisher feathers and golden shoes. She lost a shoe — and the king searched the land to find whose foot it fitted.

activities.prompt: Who helped Ye Xian?
Match the story to its detail
Similar stories can come from different countries.
What is the SAME in both stories?
options: A lost shoe helps find the heroine

thinking: Why do you think similar stories appear in places far apart?
If you set the story in your town today, what would the "lost shoe" be?
speaking: Tell someone the similarities and differences between two versions of a story you know.

project.title: Venn Diagram of Two Tales
steps: Draw two overlapping circles
Label one Ye Xian and one Cinderella
Write differences in the outer parts and similarities in the middle

lessons.title: Myths, Legends and History
objectives: Distinguish myths, legends and historical accounts
Identify features of myths and legends
explanation: A myth is a traditional story, often involving gods or supernatural beings, that explains something about the world — like why the seasons change. Many cultures have myths: Greek, Norse, Egyptian, Indian and more.
A legend is a traditional story about a hero or event that may have some basis in history, but has been exaggerated or changed over many retellings — like stories of King Arthur or Robin Hood.

History is based on evidence: documents, objects and remains. We can enjoy myths and legends as stories and also ask what evidence exists. For many people, some traditional stories are also sacred, and we treat those with respect.

context.text: Scholars use "myth" as a technical term for traditional sacred or explanatory narratives; it does not mean "false". Many communities hold their traditional stories as sacred or true, and respectful study recognises this.

vocabulary.meaning: a traditional story explaining the world, often involving gods
a traditional story about a hero, possibly based on real events
information that shows what really happened

examples: Greek myth: Persephone's time in the underworld explains winter.
Legend: Robin Hood, an outlaw hero whose real existence historians debate.

story.title: Why Persephone Brings Spring
story.text: In a Greek myth, the goddess Demeter made crops grow. When her daughter Persephone was taken to the underworld, Demeter grieved and nothing grew. A deal was made: Persephone would spend part of each year below and part above. When she returned, Demeter rejoiced and spring arrived. Ancient Greeks told this story to explain the seasons.

activities.prompt: Match the story type to its description
pairs: a hero with possible real roots

activities.prompt: What does the Persephone myth explain?
Scientists explain seasons by the tilt of the Earth as it orbits the Sun.
A legend is…
options: a story about a hero that may have some historical basis

thinking: Why did ancient people create myths to explain nature?
Can a story be meaningful even if it is not historical fact?
speaking: Retell a myth from any culture and explain what it was trying to explain.

project.title: Write Your Own Myth
steps: Choose something in nature (why the moon changes shape, why peacocks dance in rain)
Invent characters and a problem
Write a myth that explains it
Add a short note about the real scientific explanation

assessment.prompt: A story that explains thunder through a god's anger is a…
"Myth" in literature study always means a lie.
History relies on…

mastery: Distinguishes myth, legend and history with examples
Identifies typical features of myths and legends
Discusses traditional stories respectfully, separating evidence from narrative

lessons.title: Tiny Poems: Haiku
objectives: Identify the features of a haiku
Write a haiku using sensory imagery
explanation: A haiku is a short poem form from Japan. In English, haiku are often written in three lines with 5, 7 and 5 syllables.
Traditional haiku capture one moment in nature, often with a hint of the season. They use vivid images rather than telling feelings directly.
Matsuo Bashō, a famous Japanese poet of the 1600s, wrote one of the best-known haiku, about an old pond and a frog jumping in.

context.text: Matsuo Bashō (1644–1694) is widely regarded as a master of the form; the 5-7-5 pattern in English approximates Japanese sound units (on), which are not exactly the same as English syllables.

vocabulary.meaning: a three-line poem, often 5-7-5 syllables, about a moment in nature
a beat in a word
words that create pictures in the mind

examples: "Monsoon clouds roll in (5) / peacocks spread their shining tails (7) / the dry earth drinks deep (5)."
Acrostic: the first letters of each line spell a word.

story.title: The Frog and the Pond
story.text: A poet sat by an old, quiet pond. Everything was still. Suddenly — plop! — a frog jumped in, and the sound rippled out. The poet wrote just a few words about it. More than three hundred years later, people around the world still read that tiny poem and feel the quiet moment.

activities.prompt: Put the parts of writing a haiku in order
Haiku traditionally come from…
Haiku often describe a moment in nature.
Which line has 5 syllables?

thinking: Why might a very short poem be powerful?
Is it more important to follow 5-7-5 exactly, or to capture a strong image?
speaking: Read your haiku aloud slowly, then explain the moment it captures.

project.title: Haiku Nature Walk
steps: Spend five quiet minutes observing nature
Note sights, sounds and smells
Write three haiku about what you noticed
Illustrate your favourite one

assessment.prompt: How many lines in a haiku?
Middle line usually has ___ syllables.
Imagery helps readers picture the moment.

lessons.title: Who Is Telling the Story?
objectives: Identify first-person and third-person narration
Explain how point of view affects what readers know and feel
explanation: A first-person narrator is a character in the story using "I": "I opened the door and froze." We see only what they see and know only what they think.
A third-person narrator uses "he", "she", "they". A third-person limited narrator follows one character closely; an omniscient (all-knowing) narrator can tell us what everyone thinks.
Point of view shapes our sympathy and suspense. A narrator might even be unreliable — mistaken, biased, or hiding things — so readers must think critically about what they are told.

vocabulary.meaning: the voice telling the story
narration using I
knowing everything
a narrator whose account cannot be fully trusted

examples: "I knew I shouldn't open the box." — first person.
"Meanwhile, far away, the king was plotting." — omniscient third person.

story.title: The Wolf's Side of the Story
story.text: Everyone knows the tale of the three little pigs. But what if the wolf told it? "I only went to borrow a cup of sugar," he says, "and I had a terrible cold. Achoo!" Readers laugh — because a narrator telling his own story might not be telling the whole truth.

activities.prompt: Match the sentence to its point of view
pairs: Everyone secretly wondered what Ravi knew.

activities.prompt: An unreliable narrator…
A first-person narrator can know exactly what everyone else thinks.
Which pronoun shows first person?

thinking: How would a story you know change if a different character narrated it?
Why might an author choose an unreliable narrator?
speaking: Retell a well-known story from the villain's point of view to someone, then discuss how it changed.

project.title: Point-of-View Rewrite

assessment.prompt: "He wondered if anyone noticed." Point of view?

lessons.title: Stories from Indian Writers
objectives: Read and respond to works by notable Indian writers
Discuss how setting and culture appear in literature
prerequisites: Discusses themes and point of view
explanation: India has a rich literary tradition in many languages. Rabindranath Tagore wrote poems, songs and stories in Bengali and became the first non-European to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1913.
R. K. Narayan wrote in English about the fictional town of Malgudi, capturing everyday South Indian life with gentle humour; "Swami and Friends" follows a schoolboy's adventures.
Reading literature from many places lets us see the world through different eyes. Translations bring stories across languages, though some meanings, wordplay and sounds are hard to carry over.

context.text: Tagore received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913, largely for "Gitanjali". R. K. Narayan's first novel, "Swami and Friends", was published in 1935.

vocabulary.meaning: written works valued for their artistry and ideas
rendering text from one language into another
time and place of a story
a collection of works

examples: Tagore's "Kabuliwala" tells of a bond between a little girl and an Afghan fruit-seller in Kolkata.
Malgudi is a fictional town, but readers feel they could visit it.

story.title: The Kabuliwala
story.text: In Tagore's story, little Mini chatters happily with Rahamat, a tall fruit-seller from Kabul who reminds him of his own daughter far away. Years pass, and when he returns, Mini is a grown bride who no longer remembers him. Her father, seeing Rahamat's sadness, understands that fathers everywhere share the same love.

Malgudi is…
options: a fictional town created by R. K. Narayan

activities.prompt: Translations can lose some wordplay and sound of the original.

lessons.title: The Tragic Hero
objectives: Analyse the features of tragedy
Compare dramatic traditions
prerequisites: Analyses character, theme and point of view
explanation: In classical tragedy, as described by Aristotle, a noble hero falls from good fortune to disaster, often through a flaw or error of judgement (hamartia). The audience feels pity and fear, followed by a release of emotion called catharsis.
Shakespeare's tragedies — Hamlet, Macbeth, King Lear — follow and adapt this pattern. Macbeth's ambition, stirred by prophecy, leads him to murder and ruin.

India has its own classical drama. Kalidasa's Sanskrit play "Abhijnanashakuntalam" (The Recognition of Shakuntala) is celebrated worldwide. Classical Sanskrit drama theory (in the Natyashastra) emphasises rasa — the emotional flavour experienced by the audience — and the classical tradition generally avoided tragic endings.

context.text: The Natyashastra is traditionally attributed to Bharata Muni; scholars date its compilation broadly between about 200 BCE and 200 CE. Kalidasa is usually dated to around the 4th–5th century CE.
Critics debate whether "tragic flaw" is the best translation of Aristotle's hamartia; many prefer "error" or "mistake".

vocabulary.meaning: a drama ending in the downfall of the main character
the hero's error or flaw
emotional release felt by the audience
in Indian aesthetics, the emotional essence evoked in the audience

examples: Macbeth: ambition → murder → guilt → downfall.
Shakuntala: separation through a curse, then recognition and reunion.

story.title: Two Theatres, Two Feelings
story.text: A student watched Macbeth and left shaken but strangely relieved. Months later she watched a performance of Shakuntala and left uplifted, filled with longing and joy. She wondered: why did one tradition want audiences to feel catharsis through ruin, and another to savour rasa through harmony?

activities.prompt: Match the term to its meaning
pairs: emotional essence savoured by the audience

activities.prompt: Macbeth's downfall is driven mainly by…
Kalidasa wrote in Sanskrit.
Classical Sanskrit drama generally…

thinking: Why might audiences enjoy watching tragedy?
What do the differences between Greek and Sanskrit drama suggest about their cultures' values?
speaking: Perform a short soliloquy and explain what it reveals about the character's inner conflict.

project.title: Comparative Drama Essay
materials: Macbeth and an English translation of Shakuntala (or detailed summaries)
steps: Read key scenes from both plays
Note how each handles conflict, emotion and ending

Write a 1000-word comparison

assessment.prompt: Aristotle's word for emotional release is…
The Natyashastra is a work about…
A tragic hero usually begins in a position of high status.

mastery: Analyses tragic structure in a play
Compares dramatic traditions with accurate context
Writes informed comparative analysis

lessons.title: Reading Through Different Lenses
objectives: Apply at least two critical lenses to a text
Evaluate competing interpretations
prerequisites: Writes analytical essays with a thesis
explanation: Literary critics read texts through different "lenses" — sets of questions that highlight different aspects. A historical lens asks how the time of writing shaped the text.

A feminist lens asks how gender roles are portrayed and challenged. A postcolonial lens examines how colonialism and power between cultures shape stories. A reader-response lens focuses on how readers create meaning.
No single lens is "correct". Each reveals something and misses something. Strong critics test interpretations against textual evidence and remain open to others.

context.text: Critical lenses are interpretive frameworks; different scholars may reach different, well-argued conclusions about the same text.

vocabulary.meaning: a perspective used to interpret a text
relating to the effects of colonisation on cultures and literature
an explanation of meaning
circumstances surrounding a text

examples: Feminist lens on a fairy tale: why does the princess wait to be rescued?
Postcolonial lens on "Kim" by Kipling: how is India represented by a British author?

story.title: The Book Club Argument
story.text: Four friends discussed the same novel. One talked about the era it was written in; another about how women were shown; another about how colonial power appeared; the last about how the ending made her feel. At first they argued — then realised each had noticed something the others missed.

activities.prompt: Match the lens to its question
pairs: How did the time of writing shape this?
What does this mean to me as a reader?

activities.prompt: There is only one correct interpretation of a great book.
A strong interpretation is supported by…
A postcolonial lens would especially examine…

thinking: Can applying a modern lens to an old text be unfair to it? Or necessary?
Which lens do you find most useful, and why?
speaking: Lead a short discussion of a fairy tale, asking questions from two different lenses.

project.title: Multi-Lens Analysis
materials: a novel or short story studied in depth
steps: Choose a text
Write one paragraph each from three lenses
Identify evidence each lens highlights
Write a conclusion evaluating which lens is most illuminating for this text

assessment.prompt: A lens focusing on the reader's experience is…
Different lenses can reveal different meanings.
"Context" means…

mastery: Applies multiple critical lenses with evidence
